paper_title: VisualArtifactSpec 1.0: Evaluating Visual Artifacts under Task Specifications

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Visual artifact tasks test agents' ability to translate task specifications and source materials into outputs that meet practical needs. Evaluation across artifact families helps distinguish broadly applicable authoring capabilities from strengths confined to a particular medium. We introduce VisualArtifactSpec 1.0 (VAS), a benchmark of 211 creation and modification tasks spanning presentations, static graphics, animations and videos, and web interfaces. Each task specifies authoring objectives, source materials, constraints, and deliverables. Existing benchmarks provide limited support for systematically evaluating how authoring choices suit different audiences, purposes, and media across artifact families. VAS evaluates two aspects separately: Task Fulfillment verifies explicit requirements and applicable functionality, while Artifact Performance assesses Content, Organization, Visuals, and Delivery. Task-specific rating anchors instantiate shared criteria for the intended audience, purpose, and medium, with judgments grounded in source materials and artifact inspection records. We evaluate nine model-harness configurations on all 211 tasks. Overall scores range from 42.12 to 70.52, with Artifact Performance accounting for 73.4% of the gap between the highest- and lowest-scoring configurations.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Visual artifacts make an agents interpretation of task concrete and inspectable. Presentations must develop an account across slides, animations must convey changes over time, and web interfaces must support browsing and interaction. These tasks share demands for source integration, content organization, and visual communication, but place different constraints on their execution. Evaluating multiple artifact families therefore helps determine whether an agents strengths extend across deliverable forms or remain concentrated in particular medium. Table 1 compares the artifact coverage and evaluation criteria of existing benchmarks. PresentBench [Chen et al., 2026], Code2Video [Chen et al., 2025], and Vision2Web [He et al., 2026] establish detailed protocols for presentations, educational videos, and websites, respectively. ArtifactsBench extends evaluation to multiple executable artifact types, including checks of instruction compliance, functionality, visual presentation, and content accuracy [Zhang et al., 2026]. These advances leave further evaluation need: systematically assessing how authoring choices serve different audiences, purposes, and media under common framework across artifact families. Broad coverage, requirement satisfaction, and content accuracy alone do not establish whether the selected content, structure, and presentation are appropriate for the intended context. Table 1: Artifact coverage and evaluation criteria of representative benchmarks. For evaluation criteria, : routinely evaluated; : routine evaluation not established. Deﬁnitions and evidence are provided in Appendix C. Benchmark Coverage Task Fulﬁllment Artifact Performance Instruction Functional Content Audience Medium compliance veriﬁcation presentation accuracy alignment adaptation Visual StructBench [Zhuo et al., 2026] DrawAI-Bench [Cao et al., 2026] BizGenEval [Li et al., 2026] VAO-Bench [Guo et al., 2026] PresentBench [Chen et al., 2026] Code2Video [Chen et al., 2025] Vision2Web [He et al., 2026] EvoPresent [Liu et al., 2025] GDB [Deganutti et al., 2026b] ArtifactsBench [Zhang et al., 2026] VAS 1.0 G W P/M G/M G/M/W P/G/M/W Coverage. P: presentation decks; G: static graphics; M: animations/videos; W: web interfaces. Slide images, single-slide reconstruction, and static webpage renderings do not count toward or W. Audience alignment: ﬁt to audience knowledge and needs; Medium adaptation: ﬁt to medium or platform usage preferences. We introduce VisualArtifactSpec 1.0 (VAS), benchmark of 211 creation and modiﬁcation tasks spanning presentations, static graphics, animations and videos, and web interfaces. Figure 1 shows representative artifacts from these four families. Task construction pairs source materials with authoring objectives, constraints, and required deliverables, while specifying the audience, purpose, and medium that inform both authoring and evaluation. VAS evaluates two aspects separately: Task Fulﬁllment veriﬁes explicit requirements and applicable functionality, while Artifact Performance assesses Content, Organization, Visuals, and Delivery. Shared criteria are instantiated through task-speciﬁc rating anchors informed by the audience, purpose, and medium. Figure 2 illustrates why these anchors matter: with the required information retained, content emphasis can support technical analysis or product promotion (A), information organization can provide compact service overview or stepwise web guidance (B), and visual presentation can support ﬂavor comparison or lifestyle appeal (C). Judgments link the criteria to source materials and native, rendered, temporal, or interaction evidence, making unmet requirements distinguishable from weaknesses in authoring choices. 2 Figure 2: Content emphasis (A), information organization (B), and visual presentation (C) can vary while required information is retained. The paired examples illustrate authoring choices shaped by audience, purpose, and medium. Experiments with nine modelharness conﬁgurations show that high Task Fulﬁllment scores can coexist with deﬁciencies in Artifact Performance. The cross-family comparisons in Section 4.3 reveal strengths and weaknesses obscured by overall scores. The case studies in Section 5 connect score differences to evidence organization, mobile readability, and temporal consistency in the actual artifacts. Our contributions are summarized as follows: We construct VAS, benchmark of 211 source-grounded creation and modiﬁcation tasks across four artifact families, with explicit speciﬁcations of objectives, source materials, constraints, and deliverables. We develop an evidence-based evaluation protocol that separates Task Fulﬁllment from Artifact Performance, with task-speciﬁc rating anchors that instantiate shared Content, Organization, Visuals, and Delivery criteria for the intended audience, purpose, and medium. We compare nine modelharness conﬁgurations across artifact families and connect their fulﬁllment and performance differences to observable authoring choices through artifact-based case studies.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: 2.1 Visual Artifact Authoring and Benchmarks GDPval evaluates professional work products, while AnalystBench studies reports grounded in multimodal sources [Patwardhan et al., 2025, Pham et al., 2026]. For presentations, AutoPresent introduces SlidesBench; PPTAgent assesses content, design, and coherence; and DeepPresenter reﬁnes rendered outputs [Ge et al., 2025, Zheng et al., 2025, 2026]. PresentBench provides material-grounded checklists, while SlidesGen-Bench evaluates content, aesthetics, and editability [Chen et al., 2026, Yang et al., 2026]. For graphics, ChartMimic evaluates chart-to-code generation, and Paper2Poster probes information conveyed by scientiﬁc posters [Yang et al., 2025, Pang et al., 2025]. IGenBench and StructBench assess factual reliability, while BizGenEval checks commercial-image constraints [Tang et al., 2026, Image-level checks do not establish native-ﬁle editability or Zhuo et al., 2026, Li et al., 2026]. 3 Table 2: Task coverage in the VAS 1.0 release. Shares use 211 tasks as the denominator. Secondary categories are meaningful within each family and need not represent the same classiﬁcation axis across families. Family Presentations Static graphics Animations and videos Web interfaces Tasks Share Task forms 47 72 32 60 22.3% Original decks (31); template adaptation (14); existing-deck revision (2) 34.1% Posters (8); infographics and visual summaries (24); banners (10); multi-page series (30) 15.2% Animated graphics (8); animated videos (22); edited videos (2) 28.4% Content browsing (22); data exploration (16); tools and simulations (13); stateful workﬂows (9) Total 100.0% Four artifact families Figure 3: Artifact families and 14 task types across 211 tasks, using the taxonomy illustrated in the overview. Task types follow task instructions and principal deliverables. Percentages use 211 as the denominator. executable behavior. DrawAI explicitly evaluates reconstruction ﬁdelity and editability [Cao et al., 2026]; VAO-Bench assesses edits, dependent updates, and preservation through an image-only protocol [Guo et al., 2026]. Graphic-Design-Bench covers layout, typography, infographics, design semantics, and animation [Deganutti et al., 2026b]. For animations and videos, Code2Video evaluates educational videos, while EvoPresent studies academic decks and presentation videos [Chen et al., 2025, Liu et al., 2025]. Animation2Code evaluates appearance and temporal similarity; design-video metrics cover layout, motion, temporal quality, and content ﬁdelity [Ji et al., 2026, Deganutti et al., 2026a]. For websites, Design2Code evaluates screenshot reconstruction, and DesignBench covers generation, editing, and repair [Si et al., 2025, Xiao et al., 2025]. Vision2Web tests static, interactive, and full-stack development; LongWebBench evaluates long-page structure and interactions [He et al., 2026, Zhao et al., 2026]. Across families, ArtifactsBench evaluates executable visual code using source code, temporal screenshots, and task-speciﬁc checklists [Zhang et al., 2026]. VAS covers source-grounded creation and modiﬁcation of both native and executable deliverables across four artifact families. 4 Figure 4: Application purposes across 211 tasks. The inner ring shows primary purposes and the outer ring shows speciﬁc uses. Each task is counted once; percentages use 211 as the denominator. 2.2 Rubric-Based Evaluation Criterion design ranges from instance-speciﬁc quality criteria in BiGGen Bench to hierarchical requirement decomposition in PaperBench [Kim et al., 2024, Starace et al., 2025]. In visual authoring, PresentBench aggregates binary judgments on instance-speciﬁc checklists, while ArtifactsBench scores task-speciﬁc criteria covering functionality and visual quality [Chen et al., 2026, Zhang et al., 2026]. VAS separates binary Task Fulﬁllment checks from graded Artifact Performance ratings. Across artifact families, task-speciﬁc rating anchors connect shared Content, Organization, Visuals, and Delivery criteria to the intended audience, purpose, and medium, with judgments grounded in artifact evidence. Judge validation addresses different question. MLLM-as-a-Judge and Judge Anything compare multimodal judgments with human assessments; RubricEval examines criterion-level accuracy in instruction following [Chen et al., 2024, Pu et al., 2025, Pan et al., 2026].

sections.title: 3.1 Task Deﬁnition and Coverage
sections.content: Each VAS task speciﬁes an authoring objective, its intended audience, purpose, and medium, source materials, constraints, execution conditions, and required deliverables. Agents receive the instructions and inputs; evaluator-only materials provide reference facts, expected states, requirement checks, and rating anchors. Tasks cover creation, adaptation, revision, repair, and conversion, leaving content organization and presentation open within the stated requirements and modiﬁcation boundaries. Artifact families. Table 2 summarizes the 211 tasks, and Figure 3 shows their hierarchical distribution. Presentations develop an account across slides; static graphics organize information on single page or across series; animations and videos develop content over time; web interfaces support browsing, exploration, tools, and workﬂows. Classiﬁcation follows the principal deliverable objective rather than the ﬁle extension: HTML can encode slides, an animation, or website. Appendix A.1 gives classiﬁcation rules, formats, and task identiﬁers. 5 Figure 5: Benchmark construction in three stages: sources and feasibility; task and reference construction; and execution and selection. Feasibility checks and communication purposes are illustrative examples. The selection step retains 211 release tasks from 322 candidates, considering coverage, evaluability, and source diversity. Purposes and audiences. Figure 4 groups the tasks into eight application purposes, each describing what the artifact should accomplish for its users. Every task receives one primary purpose and more speciﬁc use; Appendix provides the mapping scope. Audience knowledge and needs shape the expected explanations, while medium and purpose shape information density, pacing, and presentation. For example, research communication emphasizes evidence and its limits, whereas practical guidance emphasizes actions and consequences. These distinctions inform task-speciﬁc evaluation criteria. 3.2 Task Construction Figure 5 summarizes three stages that produced 211 tasks from 322 candidates. Stage 1: Sources and feasibility. We assemble public papers, reports, datasets, manuals, and media around concrete application objectives, retaining original ﬁles and source versions. Feasibility checks use rendering, native-ﬁle inspection, reproducible calculations, and temporal or interaction checks to establish usable inputs and observable outcomes. Controlled inputs supplement public sources for revision and repair: P03 supplies an earlier report grounded in ofﬁcial disclosures, and P26 supplies an animation with deliberate defects. Stage 2: Task and reference construction. We translate source facts and application needs into instructions, input contracts, reference facts, and task-speciﬁc rubrics. Input contracts distinguish supplied ﬁles from writable outputs; references record factual checks, expected states, and acceptable modiﬁcation boundaries. Package checks verify required ﬁles, manifests, paths, and rubric structure. Source checks resolve discrepancies against originals and independently recompute required quantities; for example, P03 checks cover ﬁnancial values, native tables, and slides that must remain unchanged. Rubric revisions are versioned with their task packages. 6 Figure 6: The two-part evaluation rubric. Task Fulﬁllment allocates 50 points equally across acceptance groups, with AND within each group. Artifact Performance maps each rating to points before weighted aggregation, yielding an adjustment from 50 to +50. The total is the base plus this adjustment, without clipping. Table 3: Task-speciﬁc observation targets for V8 (scanning and temporal rhythm). Task Intended context Observation targets P80 Research-group slides P99 Public-facing mobile carousel Within-page scanning order and clear stopping points at key conclusions across eight projected slides. Entry points, density, and reading pace across ﬁve cards, including dense tables and image captions. Stage 3: Execution and selection. Agent trials expose ambiguous instructions, missing resources, observation failures, and artifact defects. Their results inform task revisions and checks of difﬁculty and score variation. Selection balances artifact and application coverage, evaluability, and source diversity. Same-source candidates are compared by their required operations and deliverables: creation and revision from the same materials can test different capabilities, whereas superﬁcial variants add little coverage. Subsequent additions address gaps in artifact forms, authoring operations, and language coverage. 3.3 Evaluation Framework VAS separates Task FulﬁllmentCompliance (CP) and applicable Functionality (FN)from Artifact PerformanceContent (C), Organization (O), Visuals (V), and Delivery (D). The former veriﬁes speciﬁed obligations; the latter assesses authoring quality through task-speciﬁc criteria within shared dimensions. Figure 6 summarizes the framework. Requirement checks. CP veriﬁes explicit requirements such as required facts, formats, modiﬁcation boundaries, and native editability. FN veriﬁes required operations and observable outcomes, including state transitions and consistency after interaction. In the current collection, FN applies to the 60 web-interface tasks; the other 151 tasks use CP for requirement checks. CP and FN items form acceptance groups, each assigned to one dimension and ﬁxed before agent comparisons. Performance criteria and contextual anchors. The 18 shared criteria comprise Content (3), Organization (3), Visuals (9), and Delivery (3), covering conceptual expression and evidence, structure and continuity, visual presentation, and usability and handoff. Table 5 deﬁnes their scopes. Taskspeciﬁc anchors translate each scope into observable qualities for the intended audience, purpose, and medium. Table 3 illustrates this for V8. The distinction from requirement checks is explicit: in P35, CP veriﬁes required samples and calculations, while C1 assesses how clearly the graphic explains means, valid sample counts, and observational limits to ﬁrst-year students. Each criterion receives an integer rating from 3 to +3. Negative ratings distinguish severe failure (3), sustained impairment of major content or processes (2), and localized substantive defects (1). Zero denotes complete basic satisfaction without substantive defects, but ordinary quality. rating of +1 denotes excellent execution with observable room for improvement; +2 requires full reﬁnement across the applicable scope, with no substantive weakness or feasible task-relevant improvement of material beneﬁt. rating of +3 additionally requires non-obvious design that resolves real task challenge and yields substantial evidenced beneﬁts beyond an equally correct, complete, and polished conventional solution. Appendix B.3 details rating evidence and item boundaries. Evidence and judgment. Evaluation freezes the submitted artifact and its ﬁle manifest, then combines source materials with rendered views, native-ﬁle inspection, temporal samples, and interaction records as required. Websites are inspected at 1440 900 and 390 844 viewports and through required actions. multimodal judge records item-level judgments with supporting pages, regions, timestamps, or interaction states, together with artifact, rubric, and judge versions. Unresolved evaluation failures remain unscored; Appendix B.1 speciﬁes missing-artifact and website-failure handling. Section 4.1 gives the judge conﬁguration. 3.4 Scoring and Reporting Task Fulﬁllment allocates 50 points equally across acceptance groups, with AND within each group. Let ai {0, 1} denote resolved No or Yes judgment and Gj the items in group j. For groups spanning CP and applicable FN, j=1 gj = 50 50 nfail, (1) gj = ai, = iGj where nfail counts failed groups. group earns its allocation only when all its items pass, irrespective of item counts or weights. Appendix B.1 deﬁnes the CP/FN dimension scores. Artifact Performance contributes signed adjustment. The total is = + . (4) Thus [B 50, + 50], with an overall range of [50, 100] and no clipping. Full fulﬁllment and ordinary performance yield 50; reaching 100 requires full fulﬁllment and maximal performance ratings. We report the base B, CP and applicable FN passed-group rates, C/O/V/D point scores, adjustment , and total separately. Summaries use equal-task means and include task counts by family and purpose, along with completed, failed, and missing evaluations. Comparisons use common valid tasks under matching rubrics and scoring protocols; item-level evidence supports diagnosis beyond aggregate scores.

sections.title: 4 Experiments
sections.content: 4.1 Experimental Setup Tasks and agents. We evaluate nine modelharness conﬁgurations on the 211 VAS tasks: 47 presentations, 72 static graphics, 32 animations and videos, and 60 web interfaces. Each conﬁguration receives the same task speciﬁcations and source materials, with evaluation rubrics withheld during authoring. All authoring conﬁgurations use their highest available reasoning setting. GPT-6 Astra, in separate session with medium reasoning, serves as the common Agent Judge. Model identiﬁers, harness versions, reasoning labels, and detailed execution protocols are provided in the released repository. 8 Figure 7: Overall performance of nine authoring conﬁgurations. The panels show total score S, fulﬁllment base B, and performance adjustment , with explicit scales and shared conﬁguration order. Exact values are listed in Table 8. Environment and protocol. Runs use isolated Accio Linux sandboxes with 7,500-second taskstage limit. Submissions, rubrics, and judge instructions are pinned for each evaluation round. TF uses the CP/FN objective groups in revision cp-fn-objectives-v2-20261114, with all child checks required to pass and equal weights across groups. Website inspection covers both 1440900 and 390844 viewports and the required interactions; other artifacts follow the corresponding nativeﬁle, rendered, and temporal inspection requirements. Retained outputs are evaluated after authoring timeouts, and infrastructure or judge faults are handled separately from artifact defects. Metrics. Following Section 3.3, we report fulﬁllment base B, performance adjustment , and total score = +, together with Content, Organization, Visuals, and Delivery (C/O/V/D). Overall means weight tasks equally. Family proﬁles use the corresponding task subsets; purpose-level summaries cover the 151 non-web tasks with task-level purpose labels. Full-dataset analyses use all 1,899 conﬁgurationtask results; ﬁxed subset of 38 tasks illustrates task-level AP distributions for all nine conﬁgurations. Detailed numerical results are provided in Appendix D. 4.2 Overall Performance Overall differences are concentrated in Artifact Performance. Figure 7 separates total scores into their two components. GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol score 70.52 and 69.37, respectively, followed by Claude Opus 5.5 at 65.03. Across conﬁgurations, mean ranges from 41.96 to 49.51, while mean ranges from 0.16 to 21.01. Of the 28.40-point total gap between GPT-6 Astra and Claude Sonnet 5, 20.85 points (73.4%) come from AP. Reporting the components separately therefore identiﬁes whether score difference primarily reﬂects unmet requirements or the quality of authoring choices. Task Fulﬁllment and Artifact Performance reveal different limitations. Task-level results further show that similar TF scores can accompany different AP outcomes. Across the full dataset, outputs with = 50 span AP adjustments from 5.55 to 25.00, revealing differences in authoring quality beyond requirement checks. Figure 8 illustrates this distinction on ﬁxed display subset of 38 tasks. Section 5 connects such differences to the underlying artifacts and task-speciﬁc criteria. 9 Figure 8: Task-level AP on 38 matched tasks. Each circle represents one conﬁgurationtask result; ﬁlled circles have = 50, and open circles have < 50. Diamonds mark means, horizontal segments span the observed ranges, and the dashed line marks = 0. 4.3 Performance across Artifact Families and Contexts Aggregate rankings conceal family-speciﬁc proﬁles. Figure 9(a) shows distinct proﬁles across artifact families. Claude Opus 5.5 scores 69.53 on static graphics but 57.05 on web interfaces; DeepSeek varies less, from 58.32 to 61.68 across the four families. GPT-6 Astra scores above 71 on presentations, static graphics, and animations/videos, compared with 67.20 on web interfaces. Crossfamily evaluation therefore reveals both broad performance and strengths associated with particular deliverable forms. Dimension proﬁles localize performance differences. Figure 9(b) shows that GPT-6 Astra exceeds 20 points in all four AP dimensions. Gemini 4 Argon scores 9.94 in Delivery but 0.33 in Content and 0.09 in Visuals; Claude Sonnet 5 has positive Organization and Delivery scores but negative Content and Visuals scores. An accessible deliverable and followable structure can therefore coexist with weaknesses in content or visual execution. Purpose-level results in Table 10 further distinguish application settings. For example, DeepSeek scores 64.19 on promotion and engagement and 57.72 on practical guidance. These descriptive proﬁles combine differences in purpose, artifact family, and task difﬁculty. The cases in Section 5 examine audience and medium adaptation through speciﬁc rubric judgments and visible evidence. 4.4 Evaluation Analysis Sensitivity to score aggregation. We vary three aggregation choices while holding artifacts and item judgments ﬁxed: linear AP map 50r/3, equal C/O/V/D weights, and itemwise TF credit in place of grouped acceptance. Table 11 reports the results. Across the eight conﬁgurations compared under all three alternatives, the conﬁguration ordering is preserved while score magnitudes change. Linear AP raises GPT-6 Astra by 7.31 points because it awards more points to +1 and +2 ratings. Equal AP weights raise Gemini 4 Argon by 2.22 points, reﬂecting its stronger Delivery and Organization scores. Itemwise TF raises Claude Sonnet 5 by 3.14 points by crediting passed checks within Figure 9: Performance proﬁles by (a) artifact family and (b) AP dimension. P/G/M/W denote presentations, static graphics, animations/videos, and web interfaces; C/O/V/D denote Content, Organization, Visuals, and Delivery. Family cells show total scores. AP cells show dimension points before weighting, with color scale centered at zero. failed acceptance groups. These changes show how the aggregation rules control the contribution of intermediate quality ratings and incomplete acceptance objectives. From aggregate scores to actionable evidence. Criterion-level statistics in Appendix D.5 identify typography and legibility (V3) as the most frequent source of negative ratings, followed by traceability and handoff (D3), graphical craftsmanship (V6), and support for claims (C2). Section 5 relates these differences to evidence grouping in research presentation, mobile reading in educational cards, and markercurve consistency in teaching animation.

sections.title: 5 Case Studies
sections.content: We compare English-language artifacts from three tasks to relate recorded scores to visible authoring choices. Each pair receives the same fulﬁllment base; the cited AP criteria explain speciﬁc differences rather than the entire aggregate score gap. 5.1 Keeping Evidence Conditions with Research Claims P01 requests an eight-slide ResNet presentation for research-group meeting. GPT-6.1 Sol and DeepSeek both receive = 50, with AP adjustments of 23.20 and 13.65. Figure 10 shows how their slides organize experimental evidence. Sol separates single-model validation from ensemble test results and attaches the protocol and split to each number. DeepSeek groups results from different settings under Evidence at equal budget with shared same depth / same parameters / same FLOPs qualiﬁer. Recovering the qualiﬁers intended scope requires returning to an earlier slide. The local organization criterion O2 therefore assigns +2 and 1. For research audience, preserving comparison conditions locally matters even when the requested results are present. 11 Figure 10: Complete P01 slides with evidence groups marked by orange dashed boxes: separate protocol labels preserve the scope of reported results (a), whereas shared qualiﬁer spans heterogeneous comparisons (b). 5.2 Adapting Complete Information to Mobile Reading P99 requests ﬁve educational cards about hurricane forecast cones for general audience reading on phone. GPT-6.1 Sol and Claude Sonnet 5 both receive = 50, but their AP adjustments are 21.65 and 5.55. Figure 11 compares their fourth cards at equal width. Sol separates the symbol classes into distinct bands with prominent deﬁnitions, while Sonnet distributes smaller explanations across denser set of panels. At the prescribed 390-pixel inspection width, Sols supporting labels 12 Figure 11: P99: the same symbol lesson at equal display width. Phone-scale inspection distinguishes small supporting labels from repeated difﬁculty reading necessary explanations; AP summarizes all ﬁve cards. remain small (V3: 1); Sonnets necessary body and legend text repeatedly falls to roughly 58 pixels across the carousel (V3: 2). The comparison illustrates medium-speciﬁc reading burden that is not resolved by including all required information, and also identiﬁes remaining weakness in the higher-scoring output. 5.3 Maintaining Correspondence through Motion P121 requests teaching animation of the ﬁrst three standing-wave modes. Both artifacts receive = 50, with AP adjustments of 22.30 for GPT-6 Astra and 5.15 for Kimi K3. In Figure 12, Astras tracked material point remains on the second-mode curve, whereas Kimis point lies below it at the same instant. The temporal inspection also ﬁnds that Kimis three markers complete four cycles each over 420 seconds, although the curves complete four, eight, and twelve. This persistent mismatch yields 2 for both visual encoding (V4) and temporal rhythm (V8); Astra receives +2 and +1. The AP judgments reveal temporal inconsistency not captured by the current TF checks, highlighting the need to verify markercurve correspondence throughout the animation.

sections.title: 6 Conclusion
sections.content: We introduced VisualArtifactSpec 1.0, benchmark of 211 source-grounded creation and modiﬁcation tasks spanning four artifact families and eight application purposes. VAS separates Task Fulﬁllment from Artifact Performance, using shared Content, Organization, Visuals, and Delivery criteria with task-speciﬁc rating anchors to assess authoring choices in context. The results reveal substantial differences in Artifact Performance that Task Fulﬁllment alone does not capture. Family and purpose proﬁles reveal differences hidden by overall means, while artifact13 Figure 12: Complete P121 frames at 6.0 seconds. Orange dashed boxes highlight the second mode, and circles mark the tracked material point: it follows the curve in Astras frame but separates from it in Kimis. Temporal evidence establishes the underlying rate mismatch. based cases connect these differences to evidence organization, mobile readability, and temporal consistency. VAS thus provides common framework for comparing authoring capabilities across artifact families and tracing performance limitations to concrete evidence. Future work should validate judge reliability and contextual ratings through human assessment and independent judges.

sections.title: B Rubric Details
sections.content: B.1 Dimension Scores and Exception Handling Acceptance groups follow objectives such as deliverable completeness, editability, source attribution, modiﬁcation boundaries, accessibility, and required operations. Explicit page or card boundaries 18 guide the reﬁnement of coarse groups; otherwise, items are grouped by acceptance objective. Each group belongs to CP or FN, with membership frozen before agent comparisons. All child items must pass for group to pass. Groups share the 50-point base equally, irrespective of their item counts; CP and FN have no separate ﬁxed point budgets. For dimension {CP, FN} with nonempty group-index set Jd, the dimension score is its passedgroup percentage: Scored = gj . jJd Jd (5) FN is omitted when no functional groups apply. For example, with ten acceptance groups, each failed group deducts ﬁve points from the base regardless of the number of failed child items. Aggregation requires valid memberships and complete, evidence-supported judgments. Missing required artifacts receive No on affected requirements when inspection establishes their absence; unresolved assessments remain unscored. website-speciﬁc exception applies when evaluator faults have been excluded and no usable website exists because the submission is missing, contains only descriptions or screenshots, or cannot run due to its own defects: all CP/FN items receive No and all performance items receive 3. Local failures affect only dependent items. This exception does not apply to other artifact families or evaluator environment failures. B.2 Shared Performance Criteria Table 5 deﬁnes the scopes of the 18 shared performance criteria. Each task instantiates these scopes through criterion wording, observation boundaries, and rating anchors tailored to its audience, purpose, and medium. Table 5: Shared scopes of Artifact Performance criteria. Task-speciﬁc anchors determine how each scope is assessed for particular artifact. ID Criterion Evaluation scope Content C1 Conceptual expression C2 Support for claims C3 Content selection Organization O1 Overall structure O2 Local organization O3 Continuity and closure Visuals V1 Visual hierarchy Composition and layout V3 Typography and legibility V4 Visual encoding V5 Contextual aesthetics V6 Graphical craftsmanship V7 Visual consistency Accurate, understandable concepts, terminology, qualiﬁcations, and references for the intended audience. How evidence, data, or observed processes support the artifacts claims and reasoning. Relevance, priorities, information density, tone, and necessary qualiﬁcations for the intended purpose. The overall explanatory, argumentative, decision, or action path. Semantic order and relationships within page, stage, node, or comparison unit. Continuity across pages or states, or coherence and closure of branches within single page. Entry points, focal content, and relative emphasis of primary and supporting information. Area allocation, grids, balance, spacing, and whitespace between information blocks. Text visibility, size, contrast, spacing, and line breaks at the intended viewing scale. Recognizable marks and reliable correspondences between visual forms, meanings, and states. Integration of visual language with the intended context, beyond color relationships alone. Contours, line widths, image crops, proportions, and local geometric or optical alignment. Stable identities, marks, styles, and content correspondences across pages, states, and formats. Continued on next page 19 ID V8 Criterion Scanning and temporal rhythm Color relationships Delivery D1 Direct usability D2 Editable structure D3 Traceability and handoff Table 5 (continued) Evaluation scope Eye movement, information reveal, dwell time, motion, and transitions. Aesthetic coordination of hue, lightness, saturation, and color-area proportions. Locating, opening, and directly using the required deliverables. Editability and organization of required native objects, resources, and materials. Veriﬁability of required sources, calculations, changes, and usage instructions. B.3 Rating Evidence and Item Boundaries Judgments identify the observed property and its location in rendered views, native-ﬁle extracts, temporal samples, or interaction records. Positive ratings explain the design choice and its beneﬁt: +1 also identiﬁes the remaining limitation; +2 requires inspection across the full applicable scope and active checks for weaknesses; +3 additionally demonstrates how non-obvious choice resolves task challenge beyond conventional solution of comparable correctness and polish. Sampling coverage is retained with the evidence. Each item is judged within its own scope. Shared evidence supports multiple ratings only when it establishes an impact within each items boundaries. For example, reading contrast concerns V3, color-to-meaning correspondence concerns V4, and color harmony concerns V9. In modiﬁcation tasks, evaluation covers permitted edits, their integration with retained content, and newly introduced defects; unchanged source defects and harmless style differences do not incur penalties. B.4 Criterion Weights Table 6 gives the weights used in Equation 3. Each rating is mapped through ϕ before weighted averaging within its dimension. Thus, equally weighted ratings of 0 and +2 yield 12.5 points, rather than the 10 points obtained by mapping their mean rating. The criterion weights sum to 100, with dimension totals matching the C/O/V/D aggregation weights. The versioned scoring implementation and score-reporting conventions are available in the released repository. Table 6: Criterion and dimension weights. Dimension Criterion weights in order Total weight Content (C1C3) Organization (O1O3) Visuals (V1V9) Delivery (D1D3) 9, 9, 7 6, 5, 4 5, 8, 7, 5, 7, 6, 3, 3, 6 4, 3, 3 25% 15% 50% 10% Benchmark Comparison Deﬁnitions and Evidence Table 1 compares authoring evaluation protocols, including generation, editing, and reconstruction. For evaluation criteria, check denotes routine assessment through shared rubric or recurring checks across relevant task categories; isolated examples are insufﬁcient. dash denotes that routine assessment is not established. The TF/AP grouping organizes this comparison and need not reproduce benchmarks original scoring structure. C.1 Coverage and Evaluation Criteria Coverage follows the evaluated deliverable: denotes complete presentation decks, static graphics, animations/videos, and interactive web interfaces. Slide images and single-slide reconstruction do not establish P; static webpage renderings do not establish W. Task Fulﬁllment. Instruction compliance checks explicit content, structure, modiﬁcation, and deliverable obligations. Functional veriﬁcation checks operations and their resulting outputs or state transitions; rendering success alone is insufﬁcient. Artifact Performance. Visual presentation covers appearance, layout, and legibility. Content accuracy covers factual and quantitative correctness, consistency of semantic relationships, and ﬁdelity to source or reference content; visual resemblance alone is insufﬁcient. Audience alignment assesses ﬁt to readers prior knowledge and needs. Medium adaptation assesses ﬁt to medium or platforms usage preferences through choices about information density, organization, pacing, and visual presentation. Prompt-level audience descriptions, responsive resizing, or general legibility alone do not establish these last two criteria. These AP columns support cross-benchmark comparison. Content accuracy is assessed within VASs Content dimension; audience alignment and medium adaptation are expressed through taskspeciﬁc C/O/V criteria. Organization and Delivery remain distinct VAS dimensions but are not independent columns in Table 1. C.2 Evidence for Table Entries Table 7 records the principal evaluation evidence and relevant scope boundaries. Paper section and table numbers refer to the cited benchmark reports. Released checklists provide additional evidence for PresentBench and ArtifactsBench. Table 7: Evaluation evidence supporting the benchmark comparison. Benchmark Evidence and scope StructBench [Zhuo et al., 2026] Atomic factual questions support content accuracy; recurring appearance and spatial-arrangement checks support visual presentation. DrawAI-Bench [Cao et al., 2026] Fidelity criteria compare text content, formula relations, and connector semantics with references (Appendix A, Table 12), supporting content accuracy alongside visual and editability checks. BizGenEval [Li et al., 2026] Text and knowledge checks assess textual and factual correctness across visual domains, alongside visual and semantic constraint checks for instruction compliance (Sec. 3.13.4). VAO-Bench [Guo et al., 2026] Content preservation, dependent-update checks, and domain-validity ratings assess content consistency alongside visual and task-requirement checks (Appendix B.3). Its slide and webpage images count as G. PresentBench [Chen et al., 2026] Code2Video [Chen et al., 2025] Material-dependent checklists assess factual and quantitative ﬁdelity; shared rubrics assess visual design. Audience checks cover explanation difﬁculty and instructional goals across presentation contexts; medium-speciﬁc reading practices are not routine separate target. The Accuracy & Depth criterion assesses the correctness of presented knowledge alongside visual quality and temporal logic (Sec. 3.3). TeachQuiz measures knowledge transfer; this alone does not establish audience or medium adaptation. Vision2Web [He et al., 2026] Required interactions and resulting states support functional veriﬁcation. Multi-resolution prototype comparisons assess responsive visual ﬁdelity (Sec. 2.1, 3.3). Continued on next page 21 Benchmark Evidence and scope Table 7 (continued) EvoPresent [Liu et al., 2025] GDB [Deganutti et al., 2026b] ArtifactsBench [Zhang et al., 2026] Deck and video evaluation covers source ﬁdelity, visual design, and narrative coherence. Its human checklist includes distance legibility (Appendix E); source ﬁdelity alone does not establish instruction compliance. Text, typography, preservation, and requested-motion checks support compliance (Sec. 7.5, Table 44). Font-size hierarchy and general M-Judge quality criteria  (Table 65)  do not establish routine content-accuracy or audience-ﬁt assessment. Scripted interactions and task checklists assess compliance, function, and visuals. Recurring checks of factual, quantitative, and conceptual content support content accuracy; device compatibility and occasional audience-speciﬁc checks do not establish the last two columns. VAS task-speciﬁc anchors. P80s research-group slides are assessed for focal claim on each projected page and pauses between pages (V1, V8). P99s social-media carousel is assessed for card-level entry points, information density, scanning sequence, and pacing across ﬁve cards (V8). These instantiate shared criteria for different readers and presentation practices.
